title: Building a Modern Resume with JSON Resume Schema
excerpt: A deep dive into the JSON Resume schema — an open-source standard for portable, version-controlled resumes. Learn how to structure your career data, render to multiple formats, and integrate with modern tooling.
content:
# Building a Modern Resume with JSON Resume Schema ## Why JSON Resume? The [JSON Resume schema](https://jsonresume.org/schema) is an open-source initiative that defines a standardized JSON format for resume data. Instead of maintaining separate Word docs, PDFs, LinkedIn profiles, and portfolio sites, you maintain **one source of truth** — a single `resume.json` — and generate everything else from it. Key benefits: - **Version control your career** — Git history becomes your career timeline - **Portability** — Export to PDF, HTML, Markdown, LaTeX, DOCX, or any custom format - **Automation** — CI/CD pipelines can regenerate your resume on every commit - **Schema validation** — Catch missing fields or typos before publishing - **Ecosystem** — Dozens of themes, renderers, and integrations exist ## The Schema at a Glance The schema defines these top-level sections: ```json { "basics": {}, "work": [], "volunteer": [], "education": [], "awards": [], "certificates": [], "publications": [], "skills": [], "languages": [], "interests": [], "references": [], "projects": [], "meta": {} } " ``` Each section has a well-defined structure. For example, a work entry: ```json { "name": "Company", "position": "Senior Engineer", "url": "https://company.com", "startDate": "2023-01-01", "endDate": "2024-12-31", "summary": "Led backend team...", "highlights": ["Scaled API to 10k RPS", "Reduced latency 40%"] } ``` ## My Implementation I maintain my resume at [nitsuah.io/resume](https://nitsuah.io/resume) with the source at [gist.github.com/nitsuah/086f7d1de6a5fd534ac4ccce226ac1d2](https://gist.github.com/nitsuah/086f7d1de6a5fd534ac4ccce226ac1d2). The pipeline: 1. **Source** — `resume.json` validated against the official schema via AJV 2. **Render** — `jsonresume-theme-modern` + `hackmyresume` for HTML/PDF output 3. **Deploy** — Netlify builds on push; the live page is a static HTML export 4. **Sync** — GitHub Actions keeps the gist and deployed site in sync ### Validation in CI ```yaml - name: Validate JSON Resume run: | npx ajv validate -s node_modules/jsonresume-schema/schema.json \ -d resume.json --strict=false ``` ### Multi-Format Generation ```bash # HTML (for web) npx hackmyresume build resume.json TO resume.html -t jsonresume-theme-modern # PDF (for applications) npx hackmyresume build resume.json TO resume.pdf -t jsonresume-theme-modern # Markdown (for GitHub profile) npx hackmyresume build resume.json TO resume.md -t jsonresume-theme-markdown ``` ## Advanced: Custom Themes & Extensions The schema's `meta` field allows arbitrary extensions. I use it for: - **Project tech stacks** — Structured `keywords` per project for filtering - **Skill proficiency** — Numeric levels (1-5) instead of plain strings - **Visibility flags** — `public: false` for sensitive entries Example extension: ```json { "meta": { "theme": "modern", "skillsFormat": "categorized", "projects": [ { "name": "9router", "keywords": ["go", "kubernetes", "grpc"], "visibility": "public" } ] } } ``` ## Integrating with Your Portfolio Since the resume is JSON, you can fetch it directly in your portfolio: ```tsx // src/app/resume/page.tsx import resumeData from '@/data/resume.json'; export default function ResumePage() { return (

{resumeData.basics.name}

{resumeData.basics.label}

); } ``` This keeps your portfolio **always in sync** with your resume — no manual updates needed. ## Tooling Recommendations | Tool | Purpose | |------|---------| | `jsonresume-schema` | Official JSON Schema for validation | | `hackmyresume` | CLI for building/converting resumes | | `jsonresume-theme-modern` | Clean, responsive HTML theme | | `jsonresume-theme-markdown` | GitHub-flavored Markdown output | | `resume-cli` | Alternative renderer with PDF support | | `ajv` | Fast JSON Schema validator | ## Gotchas & Tips - **Dates** — Use `YYYY-MM-DD` format; `endDate: null` means "present" - **URLs** — Always include `url` fields; renderers make them links - **Highlights** — Keep them concise; 1-2 lines each, action-oriented - **Skills** — Use `keywords` array for granular tagging (e.g., `["react", "typescript", "testing"]`) - **Schema version** — Pin the schema version in `package.json` to avoid breaking changes ## Conclusion JSON Resume transforms your resume from a static document into **living infrastructure**. Once set up, adding a new role or project is a single JSON edit — everything else (PDF, website, GitHub profile) regenerates automatically. The schema is mature, the tooling is solid, and the portability pays dividends every time you apply, network, or update your portfolio. --- *My live resume: [nitsuah.io/resume](https://nitsuah.io/resume) • Source: [GitHub Gist](https://gist.github.com/nitsuah/086f7d1de6a5fd534ac4ccce226ac1d2) • Schema: [jsonresume.org/schema](https://jsonresume.org/schema)*

title: Upgrading to Next.js 16 and React 19: A Complete Migration Guide
excerpt: A practical migration guide from Next.js 14 and React 18 to Next.js 16 and React 19, including the key breaking changes and fixes.
content:
# Upgrading to Next.js 16 and React 19

## Overview

This post covers a full migration path for a production portfolio app, including routing, UI library compatibility, and build system changes.

## What Changed

- Next.js moved middleware conventions toward proxy handlers.
- React 19 removed some legacy typings and tightened behavior around render trees.
- MUI v7 changed several layout APIs, requiring updates in grid-heavy views.

## Migration Checklist

1. Upgrade dependencies in small groups.
2. Fix type errors first, then runtime warnings.
3. Replace deprecated patterns before optimizing styles.
4. Validate key routes after each deploy.

## Results

After migration, the app built cleanly and route startup remained stable with Docker warm-up verification.
